# tracing - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tracing/^0.1.41/

## Expand description

A scoped, structured logging and diagnostics system.

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

`tracing` is a framework for instrumenting Rust programs to collect
structured, event-based diagnostic information.

In asynchronous systems like Tokio, interpreting traditional log messages can
often be quite challenging. Since individual tasks are multiplexed on the same
thread, associated events and log lines are intermixed making it difficult to
trace the logic flow. `tracing` expands upon logging-style diagnostics by
allowing libraries and applications to record structured events with additional
information about *temporality* and *causality* — unlike a log message, a span
in `tracing` has a beginning and end time, may be entered and exited by the
flow of execution, and may exist within a nested tree of similar spans. In
addition, `tracing` spans are *structured*, with the ability to record typed
data as well as textual messages.

The `tracing` crate provides the APIs necessary for instrumenting libraries
and applications to emit trace data.

*Compiler support:  requires *

`rustc` 1.65+[§](https://docs.rs#core-concepts)Core Concepts

The core of `tracing`’s API is composed of *spans*, *events* and
*subscribers*. We’ll cover these in turn.

[§](https://docs.rs#spans)Spans

To record the flow of execution through a program, `tracing` introduces the
concept of [spans](https://docs.rs/span/index.html). Unlike a log line that represents a *moment in
time*, a span represents a *period of time* with a beginning and an end. When a
program begins executing in a context or performing a unit of work, it
*enters* that context’s span, and when it stops executing in that context,
it *exits* the span. The span in which a thread is currently executing is
referred to as that thread’s *current* span.

For example:

```
use tracing::{span, Level};
let span = span!(Level::TRACE, "my_span");
// `enter` returns a RAII guard which, when dropped, exits the span. this
// indicates that we are in the span for the current lexical scope.
let _enter = span.enter();
// perform some work in the context of `my_span`...
```
The [ span module](https://docs.rs/span/index.html)’s documentation provides further details on how to
use spans.

Warning: In asynchronous code that uses async/await syntax,`Span::enter`may produce incorrect traces if the returned drop guard is held across an await point. See[the method documentation](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#in-asynchronous-code)for details.

[§](https://docs.rs#events)Events

An [ Event](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html) represents a

*moment*in time. It signifies something that happened while a trace was being recorded.

`Event`s are comparable to the log
records emitted by unstructured logging code, but unlike a typical log line,
an `Event` may occur within the context of a span.For example:

```
use tracing::{event, span, Level};
// records an event outside of any span context:
event!(Level::INFO, "something happened");
let span = span!(Level::INFO, "my_span");
let _guard = span.enter();
// records an event within "my_span".
event!(Level::DEBUG, "something happened inside my_span");
```
In general, events should be used to represent points in time *within* a
span — a request returned with a given status code, *n* new items were
taken from a queue, and so on.

The [ Event struct](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html) documentation provides further details on using
events.

[§](https://docs.rs#subscribers)Subscribers

As `Span`s and `Event`s occur, they are recorded or aggregated by
implementations of the [ Subscriber](https://docs.rs/trait.Subscriber.html) trait.

`Subscriber`s are notified
when an `Event` takes place and when a `Span` is entered or exited. These
notifications are represented by the following `Subscriber` trait methods:- `event`- `Event`takes place,
- `enter`- `Span`,
- `exit`- `Span`

In addition, subscribers may implement the [ enabled](https://docs.rs/trait.Subscriber.html#tymethod.enabled) function to

*filter*the notifications they receive based on

[metadata](https://docs.rs/struct.Metadata.html)describing each

`Span`
or `Event`. If a call to `Subscriber::enabled` returns `false` for a given
set of metadata, that `Subscriber` will *not*be notified about the corresponding

`Span` or `Event`. For performance reasons, if no currently
active subscribers express interest in a given set of metadata by returning
`true`, then the corresponding `Span` or `Event` will never be constructed.[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

First, add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies]
tracing = "0.1"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#recording-spans-and-events)Recording Spans and Events

Spans and events are recorded using macros.

[§](https://docs.rs#spans-1)Spans

The [ span!](https://docs.rs/macro.span.html) macro expands to a

[which is used to record a span. The](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)

`Span` struct[method on that struct records that the span has been entered, and returns a](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.enter)

`Span::enter`[RAII](https://github.com/rust-unofficial/patterns/blob/main/src/patterns/behavioural/RAII.md)guard object, which will exit the span when dropped.

For example:

```
use tracing::{span, Level};
// Construct a new span named "my span" with trace log level.
let span = span!(Level::TRACE, "my span");
// Enter the span, returning a guard object.
let _enter = span.enter();
// Any trace events that occur before the guard is dropped will occur
// within the span.
// Dropping the guard will exit the span.
```
The [ #[instrument]](https://docs.rs/tracing-attributes/latest/tracing_attributes/attr.instrument.html) attribute provides an easy way to
add

`tracing` spans to functions. A function annotated with `#[instrument]`
will create and enter a span with that function’s name every time the
function is called, with arguments to that function will be recorded as
fields using `fmt::Debug`.For example:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use tracing::{Level, event, instrument};
#[instrument]
pub fn my_function(my_arg: usize) {
    // This event will be recorded inside a span named `my_function` with the
    // field `my_arg`.
    event!(Level::INFO, "inside my_function!");
    // ...
}
```
For functions which don’t have built-in tracing support and can’t have
the `#[instrument]` attribute applied (such as from an external crate),
the [ Span struct](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html) has a

[which can be used to easily wrap synchronous code in a span.](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.in_scope)

`in_scope()` methodFor example:

```
use tracing::info_span;
let json = info_span!("json.parse").in_scope(|| serde_json::from_slice(&buf))?;
```
You can find more examples showing how to use this crate [here](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing/tree/main/examples).

[§](https://docs.rs#events-1)Events

[ Event](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html)s are recorded using the

[macro:](https://docs.rs/macro.event.html)

`event!````
use tracing::{event, Level};
event!(Level::INFO, "something has happened!");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-the-macros)Using the Macros

The [ span!](https://docs.rs/macro.span.html) and

[macros as well as the](https://docs.rs/macro.event.html)

`event!``#[instrument]` attribute
use fairly similar syntax, with some exceptions.[§](https://docs.rs#configuring-attributes)Configuring Attributes

Both macros require a [ Level](https://docs.rs/struct.Level.html) specifying the verbosity of the span or
event. Optionally, the,

[target](https://docs.rs/struct.Metadata.html#method.target)and

[parent span](https://docs.rs/span/struct.Attributes.html#method.parent)may be overridden. If the target and parent span are not overridden, they will default to the module path where the macro was invoked and the current span (as determined by the subscriber), respectively.

For example:

```
span!(target: "app_spans", Level::TRACE, "my span");
event!(target: "app_events", Level::INFO, "something has happened!");
```
```
let span = span!(Level::TRACE, "my span");
event!(parent: &span, Level::INFO, "something has happened!");
```
The span macros also take a string literal after the level, to set the name
of the span (as above).  In the case of the event macros, the name of the event can
be overridden (the default is `event file:line`) using the `name:` specifier.

```
span!(Level::TRACE, "my span");
event!(name: "some_info", Level::INFO, "something has happened!");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#recording-fields)Recording Fields

Structured fields on spans and events are specified using the syntax
`field_name = field_value`. Fields are separated by commas.

```
// records an event with two fields:
//  - "answer", with the value 42
//  - "question", with the value "life, the universe and everything"
event!(Level::INFO, answer = 42, question = "life, the universe, and everything");
```
As shorthand, local variables may be used as field values without an
assignment, similar to [struct initializers](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch05-01-defining-structs.html#using-the-field-init-shorthand-when-variables-and-fields-have-the-same-name). For example:

```
let user = "ferris";
span!(Level::TRACE, "login", user);
// is equivalent to:
span!(Level::TRACE, "login", user = user);
```
Field names can include dots, but should not be terminated by them:

```
let user = "ferris";
let email = "ferris@rust-lang.org";
span!(Level::TRACE, "login", user, user.email = email);
```
Since field names can include dots, fields on local structs can be used using the local variable shorthand:

```
let user = User {
    name: "ferris",
    email: "ferris@rust-lang.org",
};
// the span will have the fields `user.name = "ferris"` and
// `user.email = "ferris@rust-lang.org"`.
span!(Level::TRACE, "login", user.name, user.email);
```
Fields with names that are not Rust identifiers, or with names that are Rust reserved words, may be created using quoted string literals. However, this may not be used with the local variable shorthand.

```
// records an event with fields whose names are not Rust identifiers
//  - "guid:x-request-id", containing a `:`, with the value "abcdef"
//  - "type", which is a reserved word, with the value "request"
span!(Level::TRACE, "api", "guid:x-request-id" = "abcdef", "type" = "request");
```
Constant expressions can also be used as field names. Constants
must be enclosed in curly braces (`{}`) to indicate that the *value*
of the constant is to be used as the field name, rather than the
constant’s name. For example:

```
const RESOURCE_NAME: &str = "foo";
// this span will have the field `foo = "some_id"`
span!(Level::TRACE, "get", { RESOURCE_NAME } = "some_id");
```
The `?` sigil is shorthand that specifies a field should be recorded using
its [ fmt::Debug](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Debug.html) implementation:

```
#[derive(Debug)]
struct MyStruct {
    field: &'static str,
}
let my_struct = MyStruct {
    field: "Hello world!"
};
// `my_struct` will be recorded using its `fmt::Debug` implementation.
event!(Level::TRACE, greeting = ?my_struct);
// is equivalent to:
event!(Level::TRACE, greeting = tracing::field::debug(&my_struct));
```
The `%` sigil operates similarly, but indicates that the value should be
recorded using its [ fmt::Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html) implementation:

```
// `my_struct.field` will be recorded using its `fmt::Display` implementation.
event!(Level::TRACE, greeting = %my_struct.field);
// is equivalent to:
event!(Level::TRACE, greeting = tracing::field::display(&my_struct.field));
```
The `%` and `?` sigils may also be used with local variable shorthand:

```
// `my_struct.field` will be recorded using its `fmt::Display` implementation.
event!(Level::TRACE, %my_struct.field);
```
Additionally, a span may declare fields with the special value [ Empty](https://docs.rs/field/struct.Empty.html),
which indicates that that the value for that field does not currently exist
but may be recorded later. For example:

```
use tracing::{trace_span, field};
// Create a span with two fields: `greeting`, with the value "hello world", and
// `parting`, without a value.
let span = trace_span!("my_span", greeting = "hello world", parting = field::Empty);
// ...
// Now, record a value for parting as well.
span.record("parting", &"goodbye world!");
```
Finally, events may also include human-readable messages, in the form of a
[format string](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/fmt/index.html#usage) and (optional) arguments, **after** the event’s
key-value fields. If a format string and arguments are provided,
they will implicitly create a new field named `message` whose value is the
provided set of format arguments.

For example:

```
let question = "the ultimate question of life, the universe, and everything";
let answer = 42;
// records an event with the following fields:
// - `question.answer` with the value 42,
// - `question.tricky` with the value `true`,
// - "message", with the value "the answer to the ultimate question of life, the
//    universe, and everything is 42."
event!(
    Level::DEBUG,
    question.answer = answer,
    question.tricky = true,
    "the answer to {} is {}.", question, answer
);
```
Specifying a formatted message in this manner does not allocate by default.

[§](https://docs.rs#shorthand-macros)Shorthand Macros

`tracing` also offers a number of macros with preset verbosity levels.
The [ trace!](https://docs.rs/macro.trace.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/macro.debug.html)

`debug!`[,](https://docs.rs/macro.info.html)

`info!`[, and](https://docs.rs/macro.warn.html)

`warn!`[behave similarly to the](https://docs.rs/macro.error.html)

`error!`[macro, but with the](https://docs.rs/macro.event.html)

`event!`[argument already specified, while the corresponding](https://docs.rs/struct.Level.html)

`Level`[,](https://docs.rs/macro.trace_span.html)

`trace_span!`[,](https://docs.rs/macro.debug_span.html)

`debug_span!`[,](https://docs.rs/macro.info_span.html)

`info_span!`[, and](https://docs.rs/macro.warn_span.html)

`warn_span!`[macros are the same, but for the](https://docs.rs/macro.error_span.html)

`error_span!`[macro.](https://docs.rs/macro.span.html)

`span!`These are intended both as a shorthand, and for compatibility with the [ log](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.6/log/)
crate (see the next section).

[§](https://docs.rs#for-log-users)For `log` Users

Users of the [ log](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.6/log/) crate should note that

`tracing` exposes a set of
macros for creating `Event`s (`trace!`, `debug!`, `info!`, `warn!`, and
`error!`) which may be invoked with the same syntax as the similarly-named
macros from the `log` crate. Often, the process of converting a project to
use `tracing` can begin with a simple drop-in replacement.Let’s consider the `log` crate’s yak-shaving example:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use std::{error::Error, io};
use tracing::{debug, error, info, span, warn, Level};
// the `#[tracing::instrument]` attribute creates and enters a span
// every time the instrumented function is called. The span is named after the
// the function or method. Parameters passed to the function are recorded as fields.
#[tracing::instrument]
pub fn shave(yak: usize) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error + 'static>> {
    // this creates an event at the DEBUG level with two fields:
    // - `excitement`, with the key "excitement" and the value "yay!"
    // - `message`, with the key "message" and the value "hello! I'm gonna shave a yak."
    //
    // unlike other fields, `message`'s shorthand initialization is just the string itself.
    debug!(excitement = "yay!", "hello! I'm gonna shave a yak.");
    if yak == 3 {
        warn!("could not locate yak!");
        // note that this is intended to demonstrate `tracing`'s features, not idiomatic
        // error handling! in a library or application, you should consider returning
        // a dedicated `YakError`. libraries like snafu or thiserror make this easy.
        return Err(io::Error::new(io::ErrorKind::Other, "shaving yak failed!").into());
    } else {
        debug!("yak shaved successfully");
    }
    Ok(())
}
pub fn shave_all(yaks: usize) -> usize {
    // Constructs a new span named "shaving_yaks" at the TRACE level,
    // and a field whose key is "yaks". This is equivalent to writing:
    //
    // let span = span!(Level::TRACE, "shaving_yaks", yaks = yaks);
    //
    // local variables (`yaks`) can be used as field values
    // without an assignment, similar to struct initializers.
    let _span = span!(Level::TRACE, "shaving_yaks", yaks).entered();
    info!("shaving yaks");
    let mut yaks_shaved = 0;
    for yak in 1..=yaks {
        let res = shave(yak);
        debug!(yak, shaved = res.is_ok());
        if let Err(ref error) = res {
            // Like spans, events can also use the field initialization shorthand.
            // In this instance, `yak` is the field being initalized.
            error!(yak, error = error.as_ref(), "failed to shave yak!");
        } else {
            yaks_shaved += 1;
        }
        debug!(yaks_shaved);
    }
    yaks_shaved
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#in-libraries)In libraries

Libraries should link only to the `tracing` crate, and use the provided
macros to record whatever information will be useful to downstream
consumers.

[§](https://docs.rs#in-executables)In executables

In order to record trace events, executables have to use a `Subscriber`
implementation compatible with `tracing`. A `Subscriber` implements a
way of collecting trace data, such as by logging it to standard output.

This library does not contain any `Subscriber` implementations; these are
provided by [other crates](https://docs.rs#related-crates).

The simplest way to use a subscriber is to call the [ set_global_default](https://docs.rs/subscriber/fn.set_global_default.html)
function:

```
extern crate tracing;
let my_subscriber = FooSubscriber::new();
tracing::subscriber::set_global_default(my_subscriber)
    .expect("setting tracing default failed");
```
```

```
**Warning**: In general, libraries should *not* call
     `set_global_default()`! Doing so will cause conflicts when
     executables that depend on the library try to set the default later.

This subscriber will be used as the default in all threads for the
remainder of the duration of the program, similar to setting the logger
in the `log` crate.

In addition, the default subscriber can be set through using the
[ with_default](https://docs.rs/subscriber/fn.with_default.html) function. This follows the

`tokio` pattern of using
closures to represent executing code in a context that is exited at the end
of the closure. For example:```
let my_subscriber = FooSubscriber::new();
tracing::subscriber::with_default(my_subscriber, || {
    // Any trace events generated in this closure or by functions it calls
    // will be collected by `my_subscriber`.
})
```
This approach allows trace data to be collected by multiple subscribers within different contexts in the program. Note that the override only applies to the currently executing thread; other threads will not see the change from with_default.

Any trace events generated outside the context of a subscriber will not be collected.

Once a subscriber has been set, instrumentation points may be added to the
executable using the `tracing` crate’s macros.

[§](https://docs.rs#log-compatibility)`log` Compatibility

The [ log](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.6/log/) crate provides a simple, lightweight logging facade for Rust.
While

`tracing` builds upon `log`’s foundation with richer structured
diagnostic data, `log`’s simplicity and ubiquity make it the “lowest common
denominator” for text-based logging in Rust — a vast majority of Rust
libraries and applications either emit or consume `log` records. Therefore,
`tracing` provides multiple forms of interoperability with `log`: `tracing`
instrumentation can emit `log` records, and a compatibility layer enables
`tracing` [s to consume](https://docs.rs/trait.Subscriber.html)

`Subscriber``log` records as `tracing` [s.](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html)

`Event`[§](https://docs.rs#emitting-log-records)Emitting `log` Records

This crate provides two feature flags, “log” and “log-always”, which will
cause [spans](https://docs.rs/span/index.html) and [events](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html) to emit `log` records. When the “log” feature is
enabled, if no `tracing` `Subscriber` is active, invoking an event macro or
creating a span with fields will emit a `log` record. This is intended
primarily for use in libraries which wish to emit diagnostics that can be
consumed by applications using `tracing` *or* `log`, without paying the
additional overhead of emitting both forms of diagnostics when `tracing` is
in use.

Enabling the “log-always” feature will cause `log` records to be emitted
even if a `tracing` `Subscriber` *is* set. This is intended to be used in
applications where a `log` `Logger` is being used to record a textual log,
and `tracing` is used only to record other forms of diagnostics (such as
metrics, profiling, or distributed tracing data). Unlike the “log” feature,
libraries generally should **not** enable the “log-always” feature, as doing
so will prevent applications from being able to opt out of the `log` records.

See [here](https://docs.rs#crate-feature-flags) for more details on this crate’s feature flags.

The generated `log` records’ messages will be a string representation of the
span or event’s fields, and all additional information recorded by `log`
(target, verbosity level, module path, file, and line number) will also be
populated. Additionally, `log` records are also generated when spans are
entered, exited, and closed. Since these additional span lifecycle logs have
the potential to be very verbose, and don’t include additional fields, they
will always be emitted at the `Trace` level, rather than inheriting the
level of the span that generated them. Furthermore, they are categorized
under a separate `log` target, “tracing::span” (and its sub-target,
“tracing::span::active”, for the logs on entering and exiting a span), which
may be enabled or disabled separately from other `log` records emitted by
`tracing`.

[§](https://docs.rs#consuming-log-records)Consuming `log` Records

The [ tracing-log](https://crates.io/crates/tracing-log) crate provides a compatibility layer which
allows a

`tracing` [to consume](https://docs.rs/trait.Subscriber.html)

`Subscriber``log` records as though they
were `tracing` [events](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html). This allows applications using

`tracing` to record
the logs emitted by dependencies using `log` as events within the context of
the application’s trace tree. See [that crate’s documentation](https://docs.rs/tracing-log/latest/tracing_log/#convert-log-records-to-tracing-events)for details.

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-feature-flags)Crate Feature Flags

The following crate [feature flags](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-features-section) are available:

-
A set of features controlling the [static verbosity level](https://docs.rs/level_filters/index.html#compile-time-filters).
-
`log`: causes trace instrumentation points to emit`log``tracing`subscriber has not been set. This is intended for use in libraries whose users may be using either`tracing`or`log`.
-
`log-always`: Emit`log`records from all`tracing`spans and events, even if a`tracing`subscriber has been set. This should be set only by applications which intend to collect traces and logs separately; if an adapter is used to convert`log`records into`tracing`events, this will cause duplicate events to occur.
-
`attributes`: Includes support for the`#[instrument]`attribute. This is on by default, but does bring in the`syn`crate as a dependency, which may add to the compile time of crates that do not already use it.
-
`std`: Depend on the Rust standard library (enabled by default).`no_std`users may disable this feature with`default-features = false`:`[dependencies] tracing = { version = "0.1.38", default-features = false }`

```

```
**Note**: `tracing`'s `no_std` support
     requires `liballoc`.

[§](https://docs.rs#unstable-features)Unstable Features

These feature flags enable **unstable** features. The public API may break in 0.1.x
releases. To enable these features, the `--cfg tracing_unstable` must be passed to
`rustc` when compiling.

The following unstable feature flags are currently available:

- `valuable`: Enables support for recording- [field values](https://docs.rs/field/index.html)using the- `valuable`

[§](https://docs.rs#enabling-unstable-features)Enabling Unstable Features

The easiest way to set the `tracing_unstable` cfg is to use the `RUSTFLAGS`
env variable when running `cargo` commands:

`RUSTFLAGS="--cfg tracing_unstable" cargo build`Alternatively, the following can be added to the `.cargo/config` file in a
project to automatically enable the cfg flag for that project:

```
[build]
rustflags = ["--cfg", "tracing_unstable"]
```
[§](https://docs.rs#supported-rust-versions)Supported Rust Versions

Tracing is built against the latest stable release. The minimum supported version is 1.65. The current Tracing version is not guaranteed to build on Rust versions earlier than the minimum supported version.

Tracing follows the same compiler support policies as the rest of the Tokio project. The current stable Rust compiler and the three most recent minor versions before it will always be supported. For example, if the current stable compiler version is 1.69, the minimum supported version will not be increased past 1.66, three minor versions prior. Increasing the minimum supported compiler version is not considered a semver breaking change as long as doing so complies with this policy.

The leg’s transport mode. For individual-transport legs this is a
`PersonalMode` value (e.g. `"bicycle"`, parseable via
`str::parse::<PersonalMode>()`); for public-transport legs it is the mode name
from the timetable (e.g. `"Zug"`), and for transfer legs the transfer type
(e.g. `"walk"`).

```
48async fn find_trip_of_kind(
49    kind: TripKind,
50    from_id: i32,
51    to_id: i32,
52    date_time: NaiveDateTime,
53) -> Result<Option<SimplifiedTrip>, Box<dyn Error>> {
54    // The Swiss endpoint honours only one ItModeToCover per request, so the kinds
55    // are queried one at a time.
56    let trips = OJP::find_trips_with_modes(
57        from_id,
58        to_id,
59        date_time,
60        3,
61        "OJP-Example",
62        "TOKEN",
63        kind.it_modes(),
64    )
65    .await?;
66
67    Ok(match kind {
68        // First public-transport trip departing after `date_time`.
69        TripKind::PublicTransport => trips.into_iter().next(),
70        TripKind::Individual(mode) => trips
71            .into_iter()
72            .find(|t| t.legs().iter().any(|l| l.mode() == mode.as_str())),
73    })
74}
```

## Expand description

Individual (“personal”) transport mode, as defined by the OJP 2.0
`PersonalModesEnumeration`. Used with [ RequestBuilder::set_it_modes](https://docs.rs/struct.RequestBuilder.html#method.set_it_modes) to request
monomodal trips (e.g. a pure bicycle route) in addition to public-transport results.

# into-owned-trait 1.0.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/into-owned-trait/1.0.0

`IntoOwned` trait for Rust

This crate provides the [ IntoOwned](https://docs.rs/into-owned-trait/latest/into_owned_trait/trait.IntoOwned.html) trait, which converts a

*borrowed form*of a type into its

*owned form*.

## Motivation

A common pattern in performance-sensitive code is to maintain two parallel
representations of a type: a *borrowed* form that holds references into
existing data (cheap to create and copy), and an *owned* form that carries
its own heap-allocated data (can outlive the source).

```
// Cheap to push onto a stack during processing — no allocation.
// Stored in the final result — heap-allocated, lifetime-free.
let frame = Finished;
let owned = frame.into_owned;
```
[ IntoOwned](https://docs.rs/into-owned-trait/latest/into_owned_trait/trait.IntoOwned.html) gives generic code a single, uniform interface for this
conversion, regardless of how complex the borrowed type's internal
structure is.

## Built-in implementations

Two implementations are provided out of the box as convenience building blocks when implementing the trait for your own types:

- `&T`where- `T:`- `ToOwned`- `ToOwned::to_owned`])
- [`Cow<'a, T>`][std::borrow::Cow] where`T:``ToOwned``Cow::into_owned`])

- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT)or[http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT](http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT))

at your option.

# into_owned_trait - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/into-owned-trait/1.0.0/target-redirect/into_owned_trait/

## Expand description

This crate provides the [ IntoOwned](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoOwned.html) trait, which converts a

*borrowed form*of a type into its

*owned form*.

[§](https://docs.rs#motivation)Motivation

A common pattern in performance-sensitive code is to maintain two parallel
representations of a type: a *borrowed* form that holds references into
existing data (cheap to create and copy), and an *owned* form that carries
its own heap-allocated data (can outlive the source).

```
// Cheap to push onto a stack during processing — no allocation.
#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
enum EventRef<'a> {
    Started(&'a str),
    Finished(&'a str, u64),
}
// Stored in the final result — heap-allocated, lifetime-free.
enum Event {
    Started(String),
    Finished(String, u64),
}
impl<'a> IntoOwned for EventRef<'a> {
    type Owned = Event;
    fn into_owned(self) -> Event {
        match self {
            EventRef::Started(name) => Event::Started(name.to_owned()),
            EventRef::Finished(name, ts) => Event::Finished(name.to_owned(), ts),
        }
    }
}
let frame = EventRef::Finished("build", 42);
let owned = frame.into_owned();
```
[ IntoOwned](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoOwned.html) gives generic code a single, uniform interface for this
conversion, regardless of how complex the borrowed type’s internal
structure is.

[§](https://docs.rs#built-in-implementations)Built-in implementations

Two implementations are provided out of the box as convenience building blocks when implementing the trait for your own types:

- `&T`where- `T:`- `ToOwned`- `ToOwned::to_owned`
- `Cow<'a, T>`- `T:`- `ToOwned`- `Cow::into_owned`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Into](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoOwned.html)- Owned
- Conversion of a borrowed type into its fully owned counterpart.

[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! [`IntoOwned`] gives generic code a single, uniform interface for this
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! conversion, regardless of how complex the borrowed type's internal
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! structure is.
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! # Built-in implementations
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! Two implementations are provided out of the box as convenience building
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! blocks when implementing the trait for your own types:
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//!
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! - `&T` where `T: `[`ToOwned`] (delegates to [`ToOwned::to_owned`])
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! - [`Cow<'a, T>`][std::borrow::Cow] where `T: `[`ToOwned`] (delegates to
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!   [`Cow::into_owned`])
[53](https://docs.rs#53)
[54](https://docs.rs#54)use std::borrow::Cow;
[55](https://docs.rs#55)
[56](https://docs.rs#56)/// Conversion of a borrowed type into its fully owned counterpart.
[57](https://docs.rs#57)///
[58](https://docs.rs#58)/// Implement this trait for a *borrowed form* of a type—one that holds
[59](https://docs.rs#59)/// references into existing data—to produce the corresponding *owned form*
[60](https://docs.rs#60)/// that carries its own data and has no lifetime parameters.
[61](https://docs.rs#61)///
[62](https://docs.rs#62)/// The owned form is often a structurally identical type with references
[63](https://docs.rs#63)/// replaced by their owned equivalents (e.g. `&'a str` → `String`,
[64](https://docs.rs#64)/// `&'a T` → `T::Owned`).
[65](https://docs.rs#65)///
[66](https://docs.rs#66)/// # Example
[67](https://docs.rs#67)///
[68](https://docs.rs#68)/// ```rust
[69](https://docs.rs#69)/// use into_owned_trait::IntoOwned;
[70](https://docs.rs#70)///
[71](https://docs.rs#71)/// struct PersonRef<'a> {
[72](https://docs.rs#72)///     name: &'a str,
[73](https://docs.rs#73)///     age: u32,
[74](https://docs.rs#74)/// }
[75](https://docs.rs#75)///
[76](https://docs.rs#76)/// struct Person {
[77](https://docs.rs#77)///     name: String,
[78](https://docs.rs#78)///     age: u32,
[79](https://docs.rs#79)/// }
[80](https://docs.rs#80)///
[81](https://docs.rs#81)/// impl<'a> IntoOwned for PersonRef<'a> {
[82](https://docs.rs#82)///     type Owned = Person;
[83](https://docs.rs#83)///
[84](https://docs.rs#84)///     fn into_owned(self) -> Person {
[85](https://docs.rs#85)///         Person {
[86](https://docs.rs#86)///             name: self.name.to_owned(),
[87](https://docs.rs#87)///             age: self.age,
[88](https://docs.rs#88)///         }
[89](https://docs.rs#89)///     }
[90](https://docs.rs#90)/// }
[91](https://docs.rs#91)///
[92](https://docs.rs#92)/// let p = PersonRef { name: "Alice", age: 30 };
[93](https://docs.rs#93)/// let owned = p.into_owned();
[94](https://docs.rs#94)/// assert_eq!(owned.name, "Alice");
[95](https://docs.rs#95)/// assert_eq!(owned.age, 30);
[96](https://docs.rs#96)/// ```
[97](https://docs.rs#97)pub trait IntoOwned {
[98](https://docs.rs#98)	/// The fully owned type produced by [`into_owned`](Self::into_owned).
[99](https://docs.rs#99)	type Owned;
[100](https://docs.rs#100)
[101](https://docs.rs#101)	/// Converts `self` into a fully owned value, consuming it.
[102](https://docs.rs#102)	///
[103](https://docs.rs#103)	/// Implementations walk each field and convert references to owned data
[104](https://docs.rs#104)	/// (e.g. calling [`ToOwned::to_owned`] or [`Clone::clone`] as
[105](https://docs.rs#105)	/// appropriate). Fields that already hold owned data should be moved
[106](https://docs.rs#106)	/// without cloning.
[107](https://docs.rs#107)	fn into_owned(self) -> Self::Owned;
[108](https://docs.rs#108)}
[109](https://docs.rs#109)
[110](https://docs.rs#110)impl<T: ToOwned + ?Sized> IntoOwned for &T {
[111](https://docs.rs#111)	type Owned = T::Owned;
[112](https://docs.rs#112)
[113](https://docs.rs#113)	fn into_owned(self) -> Self::Owned {
[114](https://docs.rs#114)		self.to_owned()
[115](https://docs.rs#115)	}
[116](https://docs.rs#116)}
[117](https://docs.rs#117)
[118](https://docs.rs#118)impl<'a, T: ToOwned + ?Sized> IntoOwned for Cow<'a, T> {
[119](https://docs.rs#119)	type Owned = T::Owned;
[120](https://docs.rs#120)
[121](https://docs.rs#121)	fn into_owned(self) -> T::Owned {
[122](https://docs.rs#122)		Cow::into_owned(self)
[123](https://docs.rs#123)	}
[124](https://docs.rs#124)}

---

# polkadot_parachain_primitives - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/polkadot-parachain-primitives/^23.0.0/

## Expand description

Defines primitive types for creating or validating a parachain.

When compiled with standard library support, this crate exports a `wasm`
module that can be used to validate parachain WASM.

[§](https://docs.rs#parachain-wasm)Parachain WASM

Polkadot parachain WASM is in the form of a module which imports a memory
instance and exports a function `validate_block`.

`validate` accepts as input two `i32` values, representing a pointer/length pair
respectively, that encodes [ ValidationParams](https://docs.rs/primitives/struct.ValidationParams.html).

`validate` returns an `u64` which is a pointer to an `u8` array and its length.
The data in the array is expected to be a SCALE encoded
[ ValidationResult](https://docs.rs/primitives/struct.ValidationResult.html).

ASCII-diagram demonstrating the return data format:

The wasm-api (enabled only when `std` feature is not enabled and `wasm-api` feature is enabled)
provides utilities for setting up a parachain WASM module in Rust.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [primitives](https://docs.rs/primitives/index.html)
- Primitive types which are strictly necessary from a parachain-execution point of view.

# zstd - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/zstd/^0.12.4/

## Expand description

Rust binding to the [zstd library](https://github.com/facebook/zstd).

This crate provides:

- An [encoder](https://docs.rs/stream/write/struct.Encoder.html)to compress data using zstd and send the output to another write.
- A [decoder](https://docs.rs/stream/read/struct.Decoder.html)to read input data from a`Read`and decompress it.
- Convenient functions for common tasks.

```
use std::io;
// Uncompress input and print the result.
zstd::stream::copy_decode(io::stdin(), io::stdout()).unwrap();
```
- Compress and decompress data in bulk.
- Train a dictionary from various sources.
- Compress and decompress Zstd streams.

- Default compression level.

- The accepted range of compression levels.

# polkadot_node_primitives - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/polkadot-node-primitives/26.0.0/polkadot_node_primitives/index.html

## Expand description

Primitive types used on the node-side.

Unlike the `polkadot-primitives` crate, these primitives are only used on the node-side,
not shared between the node and the runtime. This crate builds on top of the primitives defined
there.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Available](https://docs.rs/struct.AvailableData.html)- Data
- This is the data we keep available for each candidate included in the relay chain.
- [Babe](https://docs.rs/struct.BabeEpoch.html)- Epoch
- BABE epoch information
- [Babe](https://docs.rs/struct.BabeEpochConfiguration.html)- Epoch - Configuration
- Configuration data used by the BABE consensus engine that may change with epochs.
- [Block](https://docs.rs/struct.BlockData.html)- Data
- Parachain block data.
- [Collation](https://docs.rs/struct.Collation.html)
- The output of a collator.
- [Collation](https://docs.rs/struct.CollationGenerationConfig.html)- Generation - Config
- Configuration for the collation generator
- [Collation](https://docs.rs/struct.CollationResult.html)- Result
- Result of the `CollatorFn`
- [Collation](https://docs.rs/struct.CollationSecondedSignal.html)- Seconded - Signal
- Signal that is being returned when a collation was seconded by a validator.
- [Erasure](https://docs.rs/struct.ErasureChunk.html)- Chunk
- A chunk of erasure-encoded block data.
- [PoV](https://docs.rs/struct.PoV.html)
- A Proof-of-Validity
- [Proof](https://docs.rs/struct.Proof.html)
- This is a convenience type to allow the Erasure chunk proof to Decode into a nested BoundedVec
- [Session](https://docs.rs/struct.SessionWindowSize.html)- Window - Size
- Type of a session window size.
- [Submit](https://docs.rs/struct.SubmitCollationParams.html)- Collation - Params
- Parameters for `CollationGenerationMessage::SubmitCollation`.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Babe](https://docs.rs/enum.BabeAllowedSlots.html)- Allowed - Slots
- Types of allowed slots.
- [Invalid](https://docs.rs/enum.InvalidCandidate.html)- Candidate
- Candidate invalidity details
- [Maybe](https://docs.rs/enum.MaybeCompressedPoV.html)- Compressed - PoV
- A type that represents a maybe compressed `PoV`
- [Merkle](https://docs.rs/enum.MerkleProofError.html)- Proof - Error
- Possible errors when converting from `Vec<Vec<u8>>`into`Proof`
- [Statement](https://docs.rs/enum.Statement.html)
- A statement, where the candidate receipt is included in the `Seconded`variant.
- [Statement](https://docs.rs/enum.StatementWithPVD.html)- WithPVD
- A statement, exactly the same as `Statement``PersistedValidationData`
- [Validation](https://docs.rs/enum.ValidationResult.html)- Result
- Result of the validation of the candidate.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DISPUTE_](https://docs.rs/constant.DISPUTE_CANDIDATE_LIFETIME_AFTER_FINALIZATION.html)- CANDIDATE_ - LIFETIME_ - AFTER_ - FINALIZATION
- How many blocks after finalization an information about backed/included candidate should be pre-loaded (when scraping onchain votes) and kept locally (when pruning).
- [DISPUTE_](https://docs.rs/constant.DISPUTE_WINDOW.html)- WINDOW
- It would be nice to draw this from the chain state, but we have no tools for it right now. On Polkadot this is 1 day, and on Kusama it’s 6 hours.
- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_FINALITY_LAG.html)- FINALITY_ - LAG
- Linked to `MAX_FINALITY_LAG`in relay chain selection,`MAX_HEADS_LOOK_BACK`in`approval-voting`and`MAX_BATCH_SCRAPE_ANCESTORS`in`dispute-coordinator`
- [NODE_](https://docs.rs/constant.NODE_VERSION.html)- VERSION
- The current node version, which takes the basic SemVer form `<major>.<minor>.<patch>`. In general, minor should be bumped on every release while major or patch releases are relatively rare.
- [POV_](https://docs.rs/constant.POV_BOMB_LIMIT.html)- BOMB_ - LIMIT
- The bomb limit for decompressing PoV blobs.
- [VALIDATION_](https://docs.rs/constant.VALIDATION_CODE_BOMB_LIMIT.html)- CODE_ - BOMB_ - LIMIT - Deprecated
- The bomb limit for decompressing code blobs.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [maybe_](https://docs.rs/fn.maybe_compress_pov.html)- compress_ - pov
- Compress a PoV, unless it exceeds the `POV_BOMB_LIMIT`

- [Babe](https://docs.rs/type.BabeRandomness.html)- Randomness
- Randomness type required by BABE operations.
- [Block](https://docs.rs/type.BlockWeight.html)- Weight
- The cumulative weight of a block in a fork-choice rule.
- [Collator](https://docs.rs/type.CollatorFn.html)- Fn
- Collation function.
- [Horizontal](https://docs.rs/type.HorizontalMessages.html)- Messages
- [Signed](https://docs.rs/type.SignedFullStatement.html)- Full - Statement
- A statement, the corresponding signature, and the index of the sender.
- [Signed](https://docs.rs/type.SignedFullStatementWithPVD.html)- Full - Statement - WithPVD
- A statement, the corresponding signature, and the index of the sender.
- [Unchecked](https://docs.rs/type.UncheckedSignedFullStatement.html)- Signed - Full - Statement
- Variant of `SignedFullStatement`where the signature has not yet been verified.
- [Upward](https://docs.rs/type.UpwardMessages.html)- Messages

[65](https://docs.rs#65)// For a 16-ary Merkle Prefix Trie, we can expect at most 16 32-byte hashes per node
[66](https://docs.rs#66)// plus some overhead:
[67](https://docs.rs#67)// header 1 + bitmap 2 + max partial_key 8 + children 16 * (32 + len 1) + value 32 + value len 1
[68](https://docs.rs#68)const MERKLE_NODE_MAX_SIZE: usize = 512 + 100;
[69](https://docs.rs#69)// 16-ary Merkle Prefix Trie for 32-bit ValidatorIndex has depth at most 8.
[70](https://docs.rs#70)const MERKLE_PROOF_MAX_DEPTH: usize = 8;

[75](https://docs.rs#75)	runtime API to retrieve the value from the runtime"
[76](https://docs.rs#76))]
[77](https://docs.rs#77)pub const VALIDATION_CODE_BOMB_LIMIT: usize = (MAX_CODE_SIZE * 4u32) as usize;
[78](https://docs.rs#78)

[81](https://docs.rs#81)
[82](https://docs.rs#82)/// How many blocks after finalization an information about backed/included candidate should be
[83](https://docs.rs#83)/// pre-loaded (when scraping onchain votes) and kept locally (when pruning).
[84](https://docs.rs#84)///
[85](https://docs.rs#85)/// We don't want to remove scraped candidates on finalization because we want to
[86](https://docs.rs#86)/// be sure that disputes will conclude on abandoned forks.
[87](https://docs.rs#87)/// Removing the candidate on finalization creates a possibility for an attacker to
[88](https://docs.rs#88)/// avoid slashing. If a bad fork is abandoned too quickly because another
[89](https://docs.rs#89)/// better one gets finalized the entries for the bad fork will be pruned and we
[90](https://docs.rs#90)/// might never participate in a dispute for it.
[91](https://docs.rs#91)///
[92](https://docs.rs#92)/// Why pre-load finalized blocks? I dispute might be raised against finalized candidate. In most
[93](https://docs.rs#93)/// of the cases it will conclude valid (otherwise we are in big trouble) but never the less the
[94](https://docs.rs#94)/// node must participate. It's possible to see a vote for such dispute onchain before we have it
[95](https://docs.rs#95)/// imported by `dispute-distribution`. In this case we won't have `CandidateReceipt` and the import
[96](https://docs.rs#96)/// will fail unless we keep them preloaded.
[97](https://docs.rs#97)///
[98](https://docs.rs#98)/// This value should consider the timeout we allow for participation in approval-voting. In
[99](https://docs.rs#99)/// particular, the following condition should hold:
[100](https://docs.rs#100)///
[101](https://docs.rs#101)/// slot time * `DISPUTE_CANDIDATE_LIFETIME_AFTER_FINALIZATION` > `APPROVAL_EXECUTION_TIMEOUT`
[102](https://docs.rs#102)/// + slot time
[103](https://docs.rs#103)pub const DISPUTE_CANDIDATE_LIFETIME_AFTER_FINALIZATION: BlockNumber = 10;
[104](https://docs.rs#104)
[105](https://docs.rs#105)/// Linked to `MAX_FINALITY_LAG` in relay chain selection,
[106](https://docs.rs#106)/// `MAX_HEADS_LOOK_BACK` in `approval-voting` and
[107](https://docs.rs#107)/// `MAX_BATCH_SCRAPE_ANCESTORS` in `dispute-coordinator`
[108](https://docs.rs#108)pub const MAX_FINALITY_LAG: u32 = 500;
[109](https://docs.rs#109)
[110](https://docs.rs#110)/// Type of a session window size.
[111](https://docs.rs#111)///
[112](https://docs.rs#112)/// We are not using `NonZeroU32` here because `expect` and `unwrap` are not yet const, so global
[113](https://docs.rs#113)/// constants of `SessionWindowSize` would require `LazyLock` in that case.
[114](https://docs.rs#114)///
[115](https://docs.rs#115)/// See: <https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/67441>
[116](https://docs.rs#116)#[derive(Copy, Clone, Eq, PartialEq, Ord, PartialOrd)]
[117](https://docs.rs#117)pub struct SessionWindowSize(SessionIndex);
[118](https://docs.rs#118)
[119](https://docs.rs#119)#[macro_export]
[120](https://docs.rs#120)/// Create a new checked `SessionWindowSize` which cannot be 0.
[121](https://docs.rs#121)macro_rules! new_session_window_size {
[122](https://docs.rs#122)	(0) => {
[123](https://docs.rs#123)		compile_error!("Must be non zero");
[124](https://docs.rs#124)	};
[125](https://docs.rs#125)	(0_u32) => {
[126](https://docs.rs#126)		compile_error!("Must be non zero");
[127](https://docs.rs#127)	};
[128](https://docs.rs#128)	(0 as u32) => {
[129](https://docs.rs#129)		compile_error!("Must be non zero");
[130](https://docs.rs#130)	};
[131](https://docs.rs#131)	(0 as _) => {
[132](https://docs.rs#132)		compile_error!("Must be non zero");
[133](https://docs.rs#133)	};
[134](https://docs.rs#134)	($l:literal) => {
[135](https://docs.rs#135)		SessionWindowSize::unchecked_new($l as _)
[136](https://docs.rs#136)	};
[137](https://docs.rs#137)}
[138](https://docs.rs#138)
[139](https://docs.rs#139)/// It would be nice to draw this from the chain state, but we have no tools for it right now.
[140](https://docs.rs#140)/// On Polkadot this is 1 day, and on Kusama it's 6 hours.
[141](https://docs.rs#141)///
[142](https://docs.rs#142)/// Number of sessions we want to consider in disputes.
[143](https://docs.rs#143)pub const DISPUTE_WINDOW: SessionWindowSize = new_session_window_size!(6);
[144](https://docs.rs#144)

[149](https://docs.rs#149)	}
[150](https://docs.rs#150)
[151](https://docs.rs#151)	/// Helper function for `new_session_window_size`.

[164](https://docs.rs#164)/// A statement, where the candidate receipt is included in the `Seconded` variant.
[165](https://docs.rs#165)///
[166](https://docs.rs#166)/// This is the committed candidate receipt instead of the bare candidate receipt. As such,
[167](https://docs.rs#167)/// it gives access to the commitments to validators who have not executed the candidate. This
[168](https://docs.rs#168)/// is necessary to allow a block-producing validator to include candidates from outside the para
[169](https://docs.rs#169)/// it is assigned to.
[170](https://docs.rs#170)#[derive(Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Encode, Decode)]
[171](https://docs.rs#171)pub enum Statement {
[172](https://docs.rs#172)	/// A statement that a validator seconds a candidate.
[173](https://docs.rs#173)	#[codec(index = 1)]
[174](https://docs.rs#174)	Seconded(CommittedCandidateReceipt),
[175](https://docs.rs#175)	/// A statement that a validator has deemed a candidate valid.
[176](https://docs.rs#176)	#[codec(index = 2)]
[177](https://docs.rs#177)	Valid(CandidateHash),
[178](https://docs.rs#178)}
[179](https://docs.rs#179)
[180](https://docs.rs#180)impl std::fmt::Debug for Statement {
[181](https://docs.rs#181)	fn fmt(&self, f: &mut std::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
[182](https://docs.rs#182)		match self {
[183](https://docs.rs#183)			Statement::Seconded(seconded) => write!(f, "Seconded: {:?}", seconded.descriptor),
[184](https://docs.rs#184)			Statement::Valid(hash) => write!(f, "Valid: {:?}", hash),
[185](https://docs.rs#185)		}
[186](https://docs.rs#186)	}
[187](https://docs.rs#187)}
[188](https://docs.rs#188)
[189](https://docs.rs#189)impl Statement {
[190](https://docs.rs#190)	/// Get the candidate hash referenced by this statement.
[191](https://docs.rs#191)	///
[192](https://docs.rs#192)	/// If this is a `Statement::Seconded`, this does hash the candidate receipt, which may be
[193](https://docs.rs#193)	/// expensive for large candidates.
[194](https://docs.rs#194)	pub fn candidate_hash(&self) -> CandidateHash {
[195](https://docs.rs#195)		match *self {
[196](https://docs.rs#196)			Statement::Valid(ref h) => *h,
[197](https://docs.rs#197)			Statement::Seconded(ref c) => c.hash(),
[198](https://docs.rs#198)		}
[199](https://docs.rs#199)	}
[200](https://docs.rs#200)
[201](https://docs.rs#201)	/// Transform this statement into its compact version, which references only the hash
[202](https://docs.rs#202)	/// of the candidate.
[203](https://docs.rs#203)	pub fn to_compact(&self) -> CompactStatement {
[204](https://docs.rs#204)		match *self {
[205](https://docs.rs#205)			Statement::Seconded(ref c) => CompactStatement::Seconded(c.hash()),
[206](https://docs.rs#206)			Statement::Valid(hash) => CompactStatement::Valid(hash),
[207](https://docs.rs#207)		}
[208](https://docs.rs#208)	}
[209](https://docs.rs#209)
[210](https://docs.rs#210)	/// Add the [`PersistedValidationData`] to the statement, if seconded.
[211](https://docs.rs#211)	pub fn supply_pvd(self, pvd: PersistedValidationData) -> StatementWithPVD {
[212](https://docs.rs#212)		match self {
[213](https://docs.rs#213)			Statement::Seconded(c) => StatementWithPVD::Seconded(c, pvd),
[214](https://docs.rs#214)			Statement::Valid(hash) => StatementWithPVD::Valid(hash),
[215](https://docs.rs#215)		}
[216](https://docs.rs#216)	}
[217](https://docs.rs#217)}
[218](https://docs.rs#218)

[222](https://docs.rs#222)	}

[583](https://docs.rs#583)/// Possible errors when converting from `Vec<Vec<u8>>` into [`Proof`].
[584](https://docs.rs#584)#[derive(thiserror::Error, Debug)]
[585](https://docs.rs#585)pub enum MerkleProofError {
[586](https://docs.rs#586)	#[error("Merkle max proof depth exceeded {0} > {} .", MERKLE_PROOF_MAX_DEPTH)]
[587](https://docs.rs#587)	/// This error signifies that the Proof length exceeds the trie's max depth
[588](https://docs.rs#588)	MerkleProofDepthExceeded(usize),
[589](https://docs.rs#589)
[590](https://docs.rs#590)	#[error("Merkle node max size exceeded {0} > {} .", MERKLE_NODE_MAX_SIZE)]
[591](https://docs.rs#591)	/// This error signifies that a Proof node exceeds the 16-ary max node size
[592](https://docs.rs#592)	MerkleProofNodeSizeExceeded(usize),
[593](https://docs.rs#593)}
[594](https://docs.rs#594)
[595](https://docs.rs#595)impl TryFrom<Vec<Vec<u8>>> for Proof {
[596](https://docs.rs#596)	type Error = MerkleProofError;
[597](https://docs.rs#597)
[598](https://docs.rs#598)	fn try_from(input: Vec<Vec<u8>>) -> Result<Self, Self::Error> {
[599](https://docs.rs#599)		if input.len() > MERKLE_PROOF_MAX_DEPTH {
[600](https://docs.rs#600)			return Err(Self::Error::MerkleProofDepthExceeded(input.len()));
[601](https://docs.rs#601)		}
[602](https://docs.rs#602)		let mut out = Vec::new();
[603](https://docs.rs#603)		for element in input.into_iter() {
[604](https://docs.rs#604)			let length = element.len();
[605](https://docs.rs#605)			let data: BoundedVec<u8, 1, MERKLE_NODE_MAX_SIZE> = BoundedVec::from_vec(element)
[606](https://docs.rs#606)				.map_err(|_| Self::Error::MerkleProofNodeSizeExceeded(length))?;
[607](https://docs.rs#607)			out.push(data);
[608](https://docs.rs#608)		}
[609](https://docs.rs#609)		Ok(Proof(BoundedVec::from_vec(out).expect("Buffer size is deterined above. qed")))
[610](https://docs.rs#610)	}
[611](https://docs.rs#611)}
[612](https://docs.rs#612)
[613](https://docs.rs#613)impl Decode for Proof {
[614](https://docs.rs#614)	fn decode<I: Input>(value: &mut I) -> Result<Self, CodecError> {
[615](https://docs.rs#615)		let temp: Vec<Vec<u8>> = Decode::decode(value)?;
[616](https://docs.rs#616)		let mut out = Vec::new();
[617](https://docs.rs#617)		for element in temp.into_iter() {
[618](https://docs.rs#618)			let bounded_temp: Result<BoundedVec<u8, 1, MERKLE_NODE_MAX_SIZE>, CodecError> =
[619](https://docs.rs#619)				BoundedVec::from_vec(element)
[620](https://docs.rs#620)					.map_err(|_| "Inner node exceeds maximum node size.".into());
[621](https://docs.rs#621)			out.push(bounded_temp?);
[622](https://docs.rs#622)		}
[623](https://docs.rs#623)		BoundedVec::from_vec(out)
[624](https://docs.rs#624)			.map(Self)
[625](https://docs.rs#625)			.map_err(|_| "Merkle proof depth exceeds maximum trie depth".into())
[626](https://docs.rs#626)	}
[627](https://docs.rs#627)}

# DisputeMessage in polkadot_node_primitives::disputes - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/polkadot-node-primitives/26.0.0/polkadot_node_primitives/disputes/struct.DisputeMessage.html

`pub struct DisputeMessage(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

A dispute initiating/participating message that have been built from signed statements.

And most likely has been constructed correctly. This is used with
`DisputeDistributionMessage::SendDispute` for sending out votes.

NOTE: This is sent over the wire, any changes are a change in protocol and need to be versioned.

#### pub fn [from_signed_statements](https://docs.rs#method.from_signed_statements)(

    invalid_statement: [SignedDisputeStatement](https://docs.rs/struct.SignedDisputeStatement.html),
    invalid_index: [ValidatorIndex](https://docs.rs/polkadot-primitives/25.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/polkadot_primitives/v9/struct.ValidatorIndex.html),
    candidate_receipt: [CandidateReceipt](https://docs.rs/polkadot-primitives/25.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/polkadot_primitives/v9/struct.CandidateReceiptV2.html),
    session_info: &[SessionInfo](https://docs.rs/polkadot-primitives/25.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/polkadot_primitives/v9/struct.SessionInfo.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self, [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.DisputeMessageCheckError.html)>

Build a `SignedDisputeMessage` and check what can be checked.

This function checks that:

- both statements concern the same candidate
- both statements concern the same session
- the invalid statement is indeed an invalid one
- the valid statement is indeed a valid one
- The passed `CandidateReceipt`has the correct hash (as signed in the statements).
- the given validator indices match with the given `ValidatorId`s in the statements, given a`SessionInfo`.

We don’t check whether the given `SessionInfo` matches the `SessionIndex` in the
statements, because we can’t without doing a runtime query. Nevertheless this smart
constructor gives relative strong guarantees that the resulting `SignedDisputeStatement` is
valid and good.  Even the passed `SessionInfo` is most likely right if this function
returns `Some`, because otherwise the passed `ValidatorId`s in the `SessionInfo` at
their given index would very likely not match the `ValidatorId`s in the statements.

So in summary, this smart constructor should be smart enough to prevent from almost all programming errors that one could realistically make here.

# DisputeMessageCheckError in polkadot_node_primitives::disputes - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/polkadot-node-primitives/26.0.0/polkadot_node_primitives/disputes/enum.DisputeMessageCheckError.html

```
pub enum DisputeMessageCheckError {
    CandidateHashMismatch,
    SessionIndexMismatch,
    InvalidValidKey,
    InvalidInvalidKey,
    InvalidCandidateReceipt,
    ValidStatementHasInvalidKind,
    InvalidStatementHasValidKind,
    ValidStatementInvalidValidatorIndex,
    InvalidStatementInvalidValidatorIndex,
}
```
## Expand description

Things that can go wrong when constructing a `DisputeMessage`.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.CandidateHashMismatch)

### CandidateHashMismatch

The statements concerned different candidates.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.SessionIndexMismatch)

### SessionIndexMismatch

The statements concerned different sessions.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.InvalidValidKey)

### InvalidValidKey

The valid statement validator key did not correspond to passed in `SessionInfo`.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.InvalidInvalidKey)

### InvalidInvalidKey

The invalid statement validator key did not correspond to passed in `SessionInfo`.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.InvalidCandidateReceipt)

### InvalidCandidateReceipt

Provided receipt had different hash than the `CandidateHash` in the signed statements.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ValidStatementHasInvalidKind)

### ValidStatementHasInvalidKind

Valid statement should have `ValidDisputeStatementKind`.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.InvalidStatementHasValidKind)

### InvalidStatementHasValidKind

Invalid statement should have `InvalidDisputeStatementKind`.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ValidStatementInvalidValidatorIndex)

### ValidStatementInvalidValidatorIndex

Provided index could not be found in `SessionInfo`.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.InvalidStatementInvalidValidatorIndex)

### InvalidStatementInvalidValidatorIndex

Provided index could not be found in `SessionInfo`.

# DisputeStatus in polkadot_node_primitives::disputes - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/polkadot-node-primitives/26.0.0/polkadot_node_primitives/disputes/enum.DisputeStatus.html

## Expand description

The status of dispute.

As managed by the dispute coordinator.

NOTE: This status is persisted to the database, any changes have to be versioned and a db migration will be needed.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Active)

### Active

The dispute is active and unconcluded.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ConcludedFor)

### ConcludedFor([Timestamp](https://docs.rs/type.Timestamp.html))

The dispute has been concluded in favor of the candidate since the given timestamp.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ConcludedAgainst)

### ConcludedAgainst([Timestamp](https://docs.rs/type.Timestamp.html))

The dispute has been concluded against the candidate since the given timestamp.

This takes precedence over `ConcludedFor` in the case that
both are true, which is impossible unless a large amount of
validators are participating on both sides.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Confirmed)

### Confirmed

Dispute has been confirmed (more than `byzantine_threshold` have already participated/ or
we have seen the candidate included already/participated successfully ourselves).

Convert a unchecked backing statement to a `SignedDisputeStatement`

As the unchecked backing statement contains only the validator index and not the validator public key, the public key must be passed as well, along with the signing context.

This does signature checks again with the data provided.

The choice here is fairly arbitrary. But any dispute that concluded more than a few minutes ago is not worth considering anymore. Changing this value has little to no bearing on consensus, and really only affects the work that the node might do on startup during periods of many disputes.

pub struct BabeEpochConfiguration {
    pub c: (
```
[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html), [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)),
    pub allowed_slots: [AllowedSlots](https://docs.rs/enum.BabeAllowedSlots.html),
}## Expand description

Configuration data used by the BABE consensus engine that may change with epochs.

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.c)

`c: (`[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html), [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html))A constant value that is used in the threshold calculation formula.
Expressed as a rational where the first member of the tuple is the
numerator and the second is the denominator. The rational should
represent a value between 0 and 1.
In the threshold formula calculation, `1 - c` represents the probability
of a slot being empty.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.allowed_slots)

`allowed_slots: `[AllowedSlots](https://docs.rs/enum.BabeAllowedSlots.html)Whether this chain should run with secondary slots, which are assigned in round-robin manner.

# BlockData in polkadot_node_primitives - Rust

## Expand description

Parachain block data.

Contains everything required to validate para-block, may contain block and witness data.

# Collation in polkadot_node_primitives - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/polkadot-node-primitives/26.0.0/polkadot_node_primitives/struct.Collation.html

`pub struct Collation<BlockNumber = `[BlockNumber](https://docs.rs/polkadot-core-primitives/24.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/polkadot_core_primitives/type.BlockNumber.html)> {
    pub upward_messages: [UpwardMessages](https://docs.rs/type.UpwardMessages.html),
    pub horizontal_messages: [HorizontalMessages](https://docs.rs/type.HorizontalMessages.html),
    pub new_validation_code: [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[ValidationCode](https://docs.rs/polkadot-parachain-primitives/23.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/polkadot_parachain_primitives/primitives/struct.ValidationCode.html)>,
    pub head_data: [HeadData](https://docs.rs/polkadot-parachain-primitives/23.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/polkadot_parachain_primitives/primitives/struct.HeadData.html),
    pub proof_of_validity: [MaybeCompressedPoV](https://docs.rs/enum.MaybeCompressedPoV.html),
    pub processed_downward_messages: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html),
    pub hrmp_watermark: BlockNumber,
}## Expand description

The output of a collator.

This differs from `CandidateCommitments` in two ways:

- does not contain the erasure root; that’s computed at the Polkadot level, not at Cumulus
- contains a proof of validity.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.result_sender)

`result_sender: `[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[Sender](https://docs.rs/futures-channel/0.3.31/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/futures_channel/oneshot/struct.Sender.html)<[CollationSecondedSignal](https://docs.rs/struct.CollationSecondedSignal.html)>>An optional result sender that should be informed about a successfully seconded collation.

There is no guarantee that this sender is informed ever about any result, it is completely okay to just drop it. However, if it is called, it should be called with the signed statement of a parachain validator seconding the collation.

`pub type CollatorFn = `[Box](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/boxed/struct.Box.html)<dyn [Fn](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/function/trait.Fn.html)([Hash](https://docs.rs/polkadot-core-primitives/24.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/polkadot_core_primitives/type.Hash.html), &[PersistedValidationData](https://docs.rs/polkadot-primitives/25.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/polkadot_primitives/v9/struct.PersistedValidationData.html)) -> [Pin](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/pin/struct.Pin.html)<[Box](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/boxed/struct.Box.html)<dyn [Future](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/future/future/trait.Future.html)<Output = [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[CollationResult](https://docs.rs/struct.CollationResult.html)>> + [Send](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Send.html)>> + [Send](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Send.html) + [Sync](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sync.html)>;## Expand description

Collation function.

Will be called with the hash of the relay chain block the parachain block should be build on and
the [ PersistedValidationData](https://docs.rs/polkadot-primitives/25.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/polkadot_primitives/v9/struct.PersistedValidationData.html) that provides information about the state of the parachain on
the relay chain.

Returns an optional [ CollationResult](https://docs.rs/struct.CollationResult.html).

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

`scheduling_parent: `[Hash](https://docs.rs/polkadot-core-primitives/24.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/polkadot_core_primitives/type.Hash.html)The hash of the relay chain block used as context for scheduling/validator assignment
to sign [ Self::statement](https://docs.rs/struct.CollationSecondedSignal.html#structfield.statement). For V3 this is the scheduling parent (may differ from
the candidate’s relay_parent). For V1/V2 this equals the relay_parent.

Anything else than [ Statement::Seconded](https://docs.rs/enum.Statement.html#variant.Seconded) is forbidden here.
